---
title: "Exercises — Long-read library preparation"
---

Pen and paper. Molarity arithmetic is part of several problems; use 650 g/mol per base pair.

# Part 1 — Molecules and handling

## E1. How much DNA is enough

A kit asks for 100 fmol of DNA. Your sample is 60 kb on average.

a. How many micrograms is that?
b. How many micrograms would you need for 8 kb DNA?
c. What does this say about a protocol written with a mass in micrograms?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Mass equals moles times length in base pairs times 650.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 100 fmol is 1.0 x 10^-13 mol. Times 60 000 bp times 650 g/mol is 3.9 x 10^-6 g, so 3.9 µg.
b. 1.0 x 10^-13 mol times 8000 times 650 is 5.2 x 10^-7 g, so 0.52 µg.
c. A mass rule fits one length. For longer DNA, the same mass is fewer molecules, and the
   library has fewer ends to adapt. Ultra-HMW preparations are therefore specified by
   starting cells, or by a total amount that already allows for the length.
:::

## E2. The clean sample with short reads

Your HMW DNA has a 260/280 ratio of 1.85 and a good yield. The run gives an N50 of 15 kb,
while a pulsed-field gel of the same stock showed most molecules above 100 kb. List three
places where the length could have been lost, and one measurement for each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
1. Mixing: vortexing or fast pipetting with narrow tips after the gel was run. Repeat the gel
   from the tube you actually used.
2. Cleanup: bead binding and elution, especially if the elution was cold or short. Compare the
   gel before and after cleanup.
3. Storage and freeze-thaw between the gel and the library. Run a gel again on the stock at
   the time of library preparation.
Absorbance ratios report purity, not integrity, so they cannot find any of these.
:::

## E3. Short molecules take over

A SMRTbell library is 90% by mass 20 kb fragments and 10% by mass 2 kb fragments. What is the
molar share of the 2 kb fragments? Why does it matter for loading?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
For 1 µg, the 20 kb fraction is 0.9 µg, which is 0.9 x 10^-6 divided by 20 000 x 650, or about
69 fmol. The 2 kb fraction is 0.1 µg, which is 0.1 x 10^-6 divided by 2000 x 650, or about
77 fmol. So the 2 kb molecules are about 53% of all molecules, from 10% of the mass. Short
molecules are loaded preferentially, so they would take most of the reads. This is why size
selection is not optional.
:::

# Part 2 — PacBio

## E4. Skipping the nuclease

A colleague proposes dropping the nuclease step from SMRTbell prep to save 15 minutes. What
molecules would be in the library, and what would they do on the instrument?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
List every molecule that ligation can leave with a free end.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Unligated inserts, inserts with only one hairpin, and leftover adapter would stay. Open
inserts cannot be read round and round, so they give single-pass reads of poor accuracy, and
adapter molecules produce reads with no insert. They compete for polymerase loading with the
good molecules, so the run yields less useful data for the same cost.
:::

## E5. Read classes in Iso-Seq

A cDNA is made with an oligo-dT primer and a TSO, then amplified with barcoded primers. For
each read, decide whether to keep it as full length: (a) 5' primer, cDNA, poly(A), 3' primer;
(b) cDNA, poly(A), 3' primer; (c) 5' primer, cDNA, 3' primer, 5' primer, cDNA, poly(A), 3' primer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Keep: both ends are present, so the RT reached the 5' end.
b. Discard as full length. The RT started at the tail but stopped early, or the RNA was cut,
   so the 5' end is not the transcript start.
c. Discard or split: two cDNAs are joined into one molecule, which cannot be a transcript.
   Chimeras like this arise in the library, not in the cell.
:::

## E6. Why arrays

A cDNA library has a mean transcript length of 2 kb. Explain why a standard SMRTbell of such
cDNA uses a polymerase read poorly, and how an array of 8 transcripts helps.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Each reaction well holds one molecule, and the polymerase can read far longer than 2 kb. A 2 kb
insert gives one transcript per well, with many passes over the same short insert. An array of
8 transcripts is about 16 kb, so the same well returns up to eight transcripts. Transcripts
are separated again in software, using the adapters between them. The saving is in sequencing
cost per transcript. The prices are the extra PCR and ligation steps, and a longer chain of
steps in which a transcript can be lost.
:::

# Part 3 — Nanopore

## E7. Pick the kit

Choose a kit for each case and say which property decides.

a. 150 ng of HMW DNA from a clinical sample, and a result is wanted the same day.
b. 6 million cultured human cells, and you want reads that cross a 400 kb satellite array.
c. 24 patient samples, each 500 ng, to be run on one flow cell.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Vendor selection charts list input, hands-on time, and typical read length for each kit.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Rapid kit, RAD114: 100 to 150 ng and almost no hands-on time. It has no cleanup, so reads
   are shorter and yield lower; that is accepted for speed.
b. Ultra-long kit, ULK114: it starts from millions of cells and keeps the cut density low so
   that reads reach hundreds of kb. Length is the deciding property.
c. Native barcoding, NBD114.24: barcodes are ligated per sample, then pooled and loaded. It
   fits the sample number and it does not need PCR.
:::

## E8. Ethanol after ligation

A student finishes the adapter ligation and then performs the usual bead cleanup with 80%
ethanol washes. The library does not sequence. Why, and what should the washes have been?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The adapter carries a motor protein. Ethanol can denature it, so the adapted DNA no longer
engages the pore properly. The ligation cleanup uses the kit's fragment buffers instead:
long-fragment buffer to enrich molecules of roughly 3 kb and longer, or short-fragment buffer
to keep all sizes. Ethanol is fine before the ligation, when there is no protein on the DNA.
:::

## E9. RNA: cDNA or direct

You want to know whether m6A sits on the same transcript copy as a specific splice variant,
using 400 ng of total RNA from human cells. Which route, and why does direct RNA still do an RT?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Direct RNA, since modifications are read from the signal of the native strand, which cDNA
discards. The RNA004 kit accepts 1 µg of total RNA, so 400 ng is on the low side and a
poly(A) selection would be needed, or the yield will be modest. The RT is still done: it
makes a cDNA strand that supports the RNA through the pore, and the cDNA strand is not
sequenced.
:::

# Part 4 — Enrichment

## E10. Cas9 enrichment

In Cas9 enrichment, all ends in the DNA are dephosphorylated before Cas9 is added.

a. What happens if you skip it?
b. What happens if the guide pair flanks the target on only one side?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Every free end in the sample, which is every molecule's end, accepts an adapter. The target
   is then one of the many molecules and enrichment is lost.
b. Only one new end exists, so adapters ligate on one side and reads start at the cut and run
   outwards through the target. Coverage of the target is one-sided, but the method still
   works; two flanking guides give both strands.
:::

## E11. Adaptive sampling arithmetic

The target is 1% of the molecules. A read that is kept takes 10 s of pore time, and a read that
is ejected takes 1 s. Compare on-target reads per pore hour with and without adaptive sampling.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Without it, every molecule takes 10 s: 360 molecules per hour, 1% on target, so 3.6 on-target
reads. With it, the mean time per molecule is 0.01 x 10 + 0.99 x 1, which is 1.09 s. That is
about 3300 molecules per hour, 1% on target, so about 33 on-target reads. The enrichment is
about 9 fold. The gain is bounded by the ratio of the two times: no target density can give more
than a 10 fold gain in this example.
:::

# Self-check

1. Why is mass a poor way to specify input for HMW DNA?
2. What does the SMRTbell nuclease step select?
3. Why does a shorter insert give a more accurate PacBio read?
4. What is the difference between a rapid and an ultra-long library?
5. Why does barcoding come before the adapter in native barcoding?
6. What does direct RNA sequence, and what is the cDNA strand for?
7. Name one wet-lab and one software way to enrich a locus.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. The same mass is fewer molecules as length increases, so fewer ends are available to adapt.
2. Closed molecules: those with no free end.
3. The polymerase passes around it more times, giving more consensus support.
4. Both use a transposase. The ultra-long kit is diluted so that each molecule is cut only a few times, and it uses precipitation instead of beads.
5. The adapter is added to the pool, so each sample must be marked first.
6. The RNA strand. The cDNA strand supports it through the pore but is not sequenced.
7. Cas9 enrichment, and adaptive sampling.
:::
